svg.title: Bias supply network — the small negative DC rail that holds EL34 grids at idle
svg.desc: From the PA-060 bias winding through the 1N4007 half-wave rectifier, the two-stage RC filter on the 7-lug terminal strip, the bias pots configured as voltage dividers, the grid stoppers, and finally to each EL34 control grid.
svg.text: Bias supply — the small negative rail that holds output tubes at idle
Bias tap → 1N4007 → two-stage RC filter → bias pots (dividers) → PC-3A (eyelets 6/21) → grid stoppers → EL34 grids (pin 5)

g.data-tooltip:
PA-060 BIAS TAP — single RED/BLK lead tapped off the HV secondary at ~50 V AC.
Not a separate winding: the return path is through the HV winding's center tap. The bias supply load is tiny (a few mA), so a simple tap is all it needs.
g.text: single RED/BLK lead on HV winding

g.data-tooltip:
1N4007 — half-wave rectifier.
Cathode (banded end) toward the transformer; anode toward the filter. This is BACKWARDS compared to a B+ rectifier — the polarity inversion is what makes the output NEGATIVE.
When the transformer swings negative, current is drawn OUT of the filter node toward the transformer, charging the cap with negative on its top plate.
The original ST-70 used a selenium rectifier here; modern kits ship a 1N4007 (step 1).

svg.text: Filter: two-stage RC on the 7-lug terminal strip

g.data-tooltip:
SEVEN-LUG TERMINAL STRIP — home of the bias filter network.
The strip's 7 lugs become a small RC network: • Lug 4 = first filter (100 µF, −65 V raw) • Lug 3 = second filter (100 µF, ~−43 V) • Lug 2 = divider return (10 kΩ to ground) • Lug 1 = ground (positive reference) • Lug 6 = jumpered to lug 1 for ground extension
The whole network sits below the chassis on a small terminal strip near the bias diode and the bias pots.

LUG 4 — first filter node.
100 µF cap (step 19, negative-on-top) + the 10 kΩ resistor to lug 3 form the first RC stage. Voltage here is the most negative point in the bias supply, ≈ −65 V, with some residual ripple.
In step 25, the bias diode's anode lands here.

100 µF FILTER CAP — electrolytic, negative-on-top.
Wired with its NEGATIVE terminal toward the bias rail (lug 4) and POSITIVE toward ground (lug 1). Opposite of B+ filter caps because this rail is negative. Polarity mistake = cap fails.
Step 19.

10 kΩ — voltage drop + filter (step 20).
Between lug 4 (first filter) and lug 3 (second filter). Together with the cap on lug 3, this is the second RC stage. Drops the rail from −65 V to ~−43 V and smooths ripple by another ~20 dB.

LUG 3 — second filter node, the CLEAN bias rail.
100 µF cap (step 21) + the previous 10 kΩ form the second RC stage. ~−43 V DC with millivolt-level ripple. This is what feeds the bias pots' top end.
In step 24 it's wired to the left bias pot's lug 1.
100 µF FILTER CAP — second stage. Same polarity as the first (neg to rail, pos to ground). Step 21.

LUG 2 — divider return point.
Connects to the bias pots' lug 3 (the 'low' end of each pot's resistance). A 10 kΩ resistor from lug 2 to lug 1 (ground) pulls this node toward ground so current can flow through the pot when the wiper is moved.
Without this return path, the pot wouldn't function as a divider.

10 kΩ DIVIDER RETURN RESISTOR — between lug 2 and lug 1 (ground). Step 22.
Provides the path for current to flow from the bias rail, through the pot, and down to ground — which is what lets the pot act as a voltage divider with an adjustable wiper.

svg.text: Distribution: bias pots as adjustable voltage dividers, one per output tube (with mod) or per channel (stock)

g.data-tooltip:
BIAS POT — voltage divider.
• Lug 1 = bias rail (~−43 V) — top end • Lug 3 = divider return — bottom end (pulled toward ground via the 10 kΩ on lug 2) • Lug 2 = wiper — adjustable output
Turning the pot moves the wiper between lug 1 (most negative) and lug 3 (less negative). The wiper voltage sets the bias on its EL34's grid. Target idle bias at the grid: ≈ −32 V.
Stock ST-70: 2 pots (one per channel). Individual-bias-pots mod: 4 pots (one per tube).

WIPER → BOARD → GRID STOPPER.
The wiper doesn't run straight to the tube: it enters the PC-3A board at eyelet 6 (left) or eyelet 21 (right), passes the on-board 270 kΩ grid resistors, and exits at eyelets 1/2/22/23 to the EL34 pin 6 tie point.
From pin 6, the 1 kΩ GRID STOPPER (at the socket itself, pin 6 to pin 5) carries the bias to the grid. It also suppresses parasitic RF oscillation. Step 37.
Bias DC + audio AC both arrive at this resistor; the resistor doesn't care which is which.

EL34 CONTROL GRID — pin 5 of the EL34 socket.
The bias voltage (≈ −32 V DC) sits here at idle, holding the tube at the design plate current. AC audio rides on top, swinging the grid above and below this quiescent point.
Four EL34s total — V2/V3 (left channel) and V6/V7 (right channel) — each with its own bias setting.

AUDIO AC arrives at the SAME grid pin via the coupling cap from the 6GH8A triode. The grid pin sums DC bias with AC signal — bias sets the operating point; AC modulates around it.
This is why a misbiased tube distorts: with the wrong DC, the AC swing pushes the tube into cutoff or saturation.

CATHODE SENSE — 15.6 Ω resistor at EL34 pin 8 develops a voltage proportional to plate current.
Measure this voltage at the front-panel Biaset socket to confirm bias is correct (target 1.56 V for 100 mA per pair). Adjust the bias pot until the cathode-sense voltage is at target.
See steps 31-36 and the bias-adjustment bring-up page.

svg.text: Bias is the smallest power network in the amp (~mA total) but the most consequential per milliwatt: get it wrong and the output tubes melt themselves within seconds.
The diode is oriented BACKWARDS compared to a B+ rectifier (cathode toward transformer), which is what produces a NEGATIVE rail.
Both cap polarities are NEGATIVE-toward-rail (opposite of B+ caps). Polarity mistake = cap failure.
